title: Coagulation and Fibrinolysis — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Blood Coagulation and Fibrinolysis lecture (Edwin F. Laing)

questions.stem: A minor vessel injury is followed immediately by a transient reduction in blood flow. Which response initiates haemostasis?
questions.why: Vessel constriction reduces early blood loss while platelets and coagulation then form a stable plug.

questions.stem: Why can a coagulation cascade respond rapidly to a relatively small initiating stimulus?
questions.why: Activated serine proteases generate more downstream active enzyme molecules, amplifying the triggering event.

questions.stem: Which feature prevents active coagulation proteases from propagating indefinitely away from the wound?
questions.why: Inhibitors neutralize activated factors and circulating blood dilutes and clears them, restricting coagulation to the injury.

questions.stem: Which enzyme class is characteristic of most activated coagulation factors?
questions.why: Most activated clotting factors are serine proteases that cleave specific peptide bonds in their substrates.

questions.stem: Which event makes a platelet plug initially form at exposed subendothelial collagen?
questions.why: Platelet adhesion to the damaged vessel surface occurs before extensive aggregation and fibrin stabilization.

questions.stem: A circulating platelet lacks which organelle despite retaining mitochondria and secretory granules?
questions.why: Platelets are anucleate cell fragments but retain metabolic machinery, granules, and membrane receptors.

questions.stem: Which group of substances is chiefly stored in platelet dense granules?
questions.why: Dense granules contain ADP/ATP, Ca²⁺ and serotonin; many adhesive proteins and growth factors reside in alpha granules.

questions.stem: Which constituent is characteristically located in platelet alpha granules rather than dense granules?
questions.why: Alpha granules carry PDGF, fibrinogen, vWF and platelet factor 4, unlike the small-molecule-rich dense granules.

questions.stem: A clot forming inside an intact circulating vessel is termed what?
questions.why: A thrombus forms within a vessel; an embolus is material that travels through the circulation.

questions.stem: How many polypeptide chains constitute one fibrinogen molecule?
questions.why: Fibrinogen is a hexamer built from two copies each of Aα, Bβ and γ chains.

questions.stem: What molecular change converts soluble fibrinogen into polymerising fibrin monomers?
questions.why: Thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides A and B, exposing polymerisation sites on fibrin monomers.

questions.stem: Why do circulating fibrinogen molecules not spontaneously polymerise efficiently?
questions.why: The negatively charged fibrinopeptide segments help maintain soluble fibrinogen before thrombin cleavage.

questions.stem: Which activated factor strengthens a fibrin clot by covalently cross-linking adjacent strands?
questions.why: Factor XIIIa acts as a transglutaminase, forming stable covalent links between fibrin molecules.

questions.stem: Which coagulation-factor complex efficiently activates factor X on platelet phospholipid surfaces?
questions.why: Intrinsic tenase consists of IXa with cofactor VIIIa, Ca²⁺ and a phospholipid surface.

questions.stem: Which enzyme directly cleaves prothrombin to generate thrombin in the common pathway?
questions.why: Factor Xa forms the prothrombinase complex with factor Va, calcium and membrane phospholipid to activate prothrombin.

questions.stem: Which coagulation pathway is initiated when tissue factor becomes available after tissue injury?
questions.why: Tissue factor binds factor VII/VIIa and initiates the extrinsic coagulation pathway.

questions.stem: Which substance can activate the contact or intrinsic pathway in an in-vitro coagulation test?
questions.why: Negatively charged kaolin or glass surfaces facilitate contact activation, whereas many inert plastics do not.

questions.stem: Why does exposure of a platelet phospholipid surface greatly accelerate clotting reactions?
questions.why: Negatively charged platelet surfaces organize Ca²⁺-dependent clotting factors into efficient enzyme–cofactor assemblies.

questions.stem: A person receiving citrate anticoagulant has blood that clots poorly in the collection tube. What explains this?
questions.why: Citrate sequesters Ca²⁺, preventing the calcium-dependent assembly of coagulation complexes.

questions.stem: What is the essential biochemical effect of vitamin K on coagulation factors II, VII, IX and X?
questions.why: Vitamin K supports γ-carboxylation of selected glutamate residues, creating Gla residues able to bind Ca²⁺.

questions.stem: Why is gamma-carboxyglutamate particularly important for factor activation?
questions.why: Gamma-carboxylated glutamate chelates Ca²⁺, allowing vitamin K-dependent factors to associate with phospholipid surfaces.

questions.stem: A newborn develops bleeding related to reduced vitamin K availability. Which impairment is most direct?
questions.why: Vitamin K deficiency impairs formation of functional, calcium-binding clotting factors and is a recognized neonatal bleeding risk.

questions.stem: Why can obstructive jaundice produce a tendency to bleed?
questions.why: Reduced intestinal bile salts impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K needed for clotting-factor maturation.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent haemarthroses and markedly impaired factor VIII function. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.why: Haemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency; bleeding into joints is a characteristic severe manifestation.

questions.stem: Which deficiency is responsible for classical haemophilia B?
questions.why: Haemophilia B results from factor IX deficiency, whereas haemophilia A results from factor VIII deficiency.

questions.stem: How does von Willebrand factor contribute to primary haemostasis?
questions.why: von Willebrand factor promotes platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelium and also carries/stabilizes factor VIII.

questions.stem: What additional coagulation role is performed by von Willebrand factor?
questions.why: vWF protects factor VIII in circulation; it is an adhesive glycoprotein, not a coagulation enzyme.

questions.stem: Defective vWF causes bleeding despite an intact fibrinogen molecule. Which defect best explains the early haemostatic problem?
questions.why: vWF deficiency reduces efficient platelet tethering to injured vascular surfaces.

questions.stem: Which plasma enzyme digests cross-linked fibrin into smaller degradation products?
questions.why: Plasmin is the fibrinolytic protease that cleaves fibrin and dissolves established clots.

questions.stem: Which inactive precursor is converted to plasmin during fibrinolysis?
questions.why: Plasminogen is a circulating zymogen; tissue plasminogen activator and urokinase can activate it.

questions.stem: Why does tissue plasminogen activator preferentially promote lysis at a clot?

options.label: C
options.text: It is stored in dense granules

questions.why: tPA interacts with fibrin-bound plasminogen, promoting plasmin generation near the fibrin clot.

questions.stem: Which enzyme in blood and urine can catalyse plasminogen activation?
questions.why: Urokinase is a plasminogen activator and can initiate fibrin breakdown by generating plasmin.

questions.stem: What is the anticoagulant action of antithrombin III?
questions.why: Antithrombin forms inhibitory complexes with thrombin and several other activated clotting proteases.

questions.stem: Why does heparin markedly enhance the physiological anticoagulant effect of antithrombin?
questions.why: Heparin binds antithrombin and increases its inhibitory action against thrombin and other serine proteases.

questions.stem: Which coagulation factors are among the targets inhibited by heparin-enhanced antithrombin?

options.label: B
options.text: Protein C and inactive factor VIII

questions.why: Antithrombin inhibits IIa and Xa particularly, as well as other activated proteases such as IXa and XIa.

questions.stem: Why do activated clotting factors have a short effective lifetime in circulating blood?
questions.why: Blood flow dilutes active factors; plasma inhibitors neutralize them, and organs including the liver help clear them.

questions.stem: Which product of plasmin action provides evidence that fibrin has been degraded?
questions.why: Plasmin cleaves fibrin into soluble fibrin degradation products; cross-linked fibrin degradation produces D-dimer.

questions.stem: Beyond fibrin, plasmin can degrade which group of clotting proteins?
questions.why: The lecture also identifies factors V, VIII and XIII as susceptible to plasmin-mediated proteolysis.

questions.stem: How does low-dose aspirin impair platelet aggregation?
questions.why: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, suppressing thromboxane A₂ generation for the platelet lifespan.

questions.stem: Which platelet-derived mediator is reduced when aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase-1?
questions.why: Thromboxane A₂ promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction; its synthesis depends on COX-1 products.

questions.stem: A fibrinolytic drug is given to dissolve an existing fibrin-rich thrombus. Which mechanism is intended?
questions.why: Thrombolytics such as streptokinase and tPA facilitate plasmin generation, degrading the fibrin network of an established clot.

questions.stem: Kallikrein contributes to inflammation by releasing which vasoactive peptide?
questions.why: Kallikrein acts on kininogen to generate bradykinin, which promotes vasodilation and vascular permeability.

questions.stem: Which activation event connects the contact system with intrinsic coagulation?
questions.why: The contact system involves factor XII (Hageman factor), prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen.
